---
title: "Heterogeneous treatment effects"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

An average effect can hide groups that gain a lot and groups that gain nothing. This article
estimates how a treatment effect varies with the covariates, with the tools of dmlrs:

* the best linear predictor of the effect and group average effects of a DML fit, `cate()` and
  `gate()`;
* CATE meta-learners, `cate_learner()`;
* causal forests, `causal_forest()`;
* prediction intervals for the effect on an individual unit, `conformal_ite()`;
* and, for a continuous treatment, dose-response curves, `dml_dose_response()`.

```{r}
library(dmlrs)
```

## Simulated data

A binary treatment `d`, assigned with a probability that depends on `x1`, and an effect
`1 + x2` that grows with the second covariate. Half of the units have an effect above 1 and some
have a negative one.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n <- 3000
x <- matrix(rnorm(n * 5), n, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:5)))
d <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.5 * x[, 1]))
tau <- 1 + x[, 2]
y <- d * tau + x[, 1] + 0.5 * x[, 3] + rnorm(n)
```

## Best linear predictor and group effects

Start with the average effect, from the interactive regression model.

```{r}
irm <- dml_irm(y, d, x, ml_g = lrn_random_forest(n_estimators = 200, min_samples_leaf = 5),
               ml_m = lrn_logistic_cv())
irm
```

`cate()` regresses the doubly robust signal of the effect on a basis of the covariates. The
coefficients are the best linear approximation of the effect, with valid standard errors even
though the signal comes from machine learning fits (Semenova and Chernozhukov, 2021). Here the
truth is `1 + x2`:

```{r}
blp <- cate(irm, cbind(intercept = 1, x2 = x[, "x2"]))
blp
```

`predict()` gives the effect at new points; `interval = "joint"` makes the intervals hold at all
points at once.

```{r}
grid <- seq(-2, 2, by = 0.5)
band <- predict(blp, cbind(1, grid), interval = "joint")
plot(grid, band$estimate, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = range(band), xlab = "x2", ylab = "effect")
lines(grid, band$lower, lty = 2)
lines(grid, band$upper, lty = 2)
abline(a = 1, b = 1, col = "grey50")
```

`gate()` estimates the average effect in groups, here the terciles of `x2`:

```{r}
terciles <- cut(x[, "x2"], quantile(x[, "x2"], 0:3 / 3), include.lowest = TRUE,
                labels = c("low", "middle", "high"))
gate(irm, terciles)
```

## Meta-learners

The meta-learners estimate the effect function itself. The DR-learner regresses the doubly
robust pseudo-outcome on the covariates with any learner, and supports the same inference.

```{r}
dr <- cate_learner(y, d, x, method = "DR",
                   ml_outcome = lrn_random_forest(n_estimators = 200, min_samples_leaf = 5),
                   ml_propensity = lrn_logistic_cv(),
                   ml_effect = lrn_random_forest(n_estimators = 200, min_samples_leaf = 20))
dr
cor(dr$effect, tau)
```

## Causal forests

A causal forest (Athey, Tibshirani and Wager, 2019) splits on the heterogeneity of the effect
and gives a standard error for every prediction. `test_calibration()` checks whether its
predictions carry real heterogeneity: a `differential.forest.prediction` coefficient
significantly above 0 says they do.

```{r}
cf <- causal_forest(y, d, x, ml_y = lrn_random_forest(n_estimators = 200, min_samples_leaf = 5),
                    ml_d = lrn_logistic_cv(), num_trees = 1000)
cf
average_treatment_effect(cf)
test_calibration(cf)
```

The out-of-bag predictions follow the true effect:

```{r}
plot(x[, "x2"], cf$predictions, pch = 16, cex = 0.4, col = "#0173B280", xlab = "x2",
     ylab = "estimated effect")
abline(a = 1, b = 1, col = "grey30", lwd = 2)
```

## Intervals for individual effects

The intervals above are for average effects among units with the same covariates. The effect
on one unit, `Y(1) - Y(0)`, also includes that unit's noise. `conformal_ite()` gives intervals
that cover it with probability at least 1 - alpha (Lei and Candes, 2021). With quantile forests
as score learners, the intervals adapt to the noise level.

```{r}
conformal <- conformal_ite(y, d, x, ml_lower = lrn_quantile_forest(0.05, n_estimators = 500),
                           ml_upper = lrn_quantile_forest(0.95, n_estimators = 500),
                           ml_m = lrn_logistic_cv())
predict(conformal, x[1:5, ], alpha = 0.1)
```

## A continuous treatment

For a continuous treatment, `dml_dose_response()` estimates the average outcome `E[Y(t)]` at
each dose `t` (Colangelo and Lee, 2023).

```{r}
dose <- 0.5 * x[, 1] + rnorm(n)
y_dose <- sin(dose) + x[, 1] + rnorm(n)
curve <- dml_dose_response(y_dose, dose, x,
                           ml_g = lrn_random_forest(n_estimators = 200, min_samples_leaf = 5),
                           ml_m = lrn_lasso_cv(), grid = seq(-1.5, 1.5, by = 0.5))
plot(curve)
lines(curve$grid, sin(curve$grid), col = "grey30", lty = 2)
dose_contrast(curve, reference = 0)
```

## References

* Athey, S., Tibshirani, J. and Wager, S. (2019). Generalized random forests. *Annals of
  Statistics* 47(2).
* Colangelo, K. and Lee, Y.-Y. (2023). Double debiased machine learning nonparametric inference
  with continuous treatments. arXiv:2004.03036.
* Kennedy, E. H. (2023). Towards optimal doubly robust estimation of heterogeneous causal effects.
  *Electronic Journal of Statistics* 17(2).
* Lei, L. and Candes, E. J. (2021). Conformal inference of counterfactuals and individual
  treatment effects. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B* 83(5).
* Semenova, V. and Chernozhukov, V. (2021). Debiased machine learning of conditional average
  treatment effects and other causal functions. *The Econometrics Journal* 24(2).
